call transcript post Add call summary post Add call recording post Update call status patch Copy Page Introduction Here is Front's Core API, a backend API that gives comprehensive control over all entities in Front from Contacts to Comments. Guides Refer to the following guides to learn how to use the Core API: Getting Started Fundamentals Tools Sample Application API Terminology 101 Authentication Front supports OAuth2.0 as well as API Tokens. To learn about authenticating with Front, see our guide on authentication . Base URL API calls will always work with https://api2.frontapp.com as the base URL. However, the API may return resource URLs that include your company's name, such as https://acme.api.frontapp.com . If the API is returning URLs like those, you can call it either with api2.frontapp.com or acme.api.frontapp.com . Rate Limits To ensure an acceptable response time from our API and facilitate access for all customers, Front implements an overall rate limit as well as several "burst" limits for certain endpoints. For more on these limits, please see here . Content Type The API is designed to communicate with your server using JSON. All responses coming from the API will send data in a valid JSON object. If you need to send data to the API, your request should set the Content-Type HTTP header to application/json. Some endpoints also support multipart requests for file upload. For more details about it, please check our multipart request documentation . Search parameters For some requests to get a large collection of resources, you can send search criteria in the query string via a parameter named q . Parameters for Conversations Parameters for Events Parameters for Contacts File Upload When you want to send files through the API, your request needs to be sent using the Content-Type HTTP header set to multipart/form-data. The JSON data you would normally send in the request body needs to be split in multiple form fields (one for each property) named after the property key. If the property is an array, the name should include the index of the data (ie: {"to": [ [email protected] , [email protected] ]} would be split in two fields named to[0], to[1]). 📘 Restriction on files (type and size) depends on the endpoint. If your request doesn't comply to those limitations, the response will contain an error describing the issue. Dates All dates in the Front API are encoded as a number representing Unix time: It is the number of seconds that have elapsed since 00:00:00 UTC, January 1st 1970. Since Front is based on events that can occur during the same second, all the timestamps include leap seconds with a precision of 3 digits: 1454453901.012 . Deprecation Policy Read our deprecation policy to learn how Front communicates about changes that may affect your integrations. This means you’ll need to pass your API token in the header of your request: Copy Authorization: Bearer <token> Generate an API token in the Pylon dashboard . API regions Pylon’s API is available in two regions. Use the base URL that matches where your Pylon tenant is hosted: US region: https://api.usepylon.com EU region: https://api.eu.usepylon.com Both regions use the same API endpoints and authentication. Configure your integration to use the region where your Pylon tenant is hosted. You can tell a token's region from its prefix: Prefix Region pylon_api_eu_ EU pylon_api_ US Tokens created before prefixes were introduced have no prefix. Sending a token to the other region's API returns 401 with the wrong_region_token error code, and the message names the correct URL. Once you've created a token, call the /me endpoint to retrieve details about your organization and confirm your token works. Create an API token Only Admins can create and manage API tokens. Go to Settings > Integrations & dev > API . On the Tokens tab, click Create API Token . Enter a Name . Choose who the token acts as: Leave Act as user or bot (optional) empty to give the token its own identity. Pick a Role to control what it can access, and optionally upload an icon. Or select a teammate or bot. The token uses that user's current role and permissions. Optionally, add an IP allowlist (see below). Click Create and copy the token. Pylon shows it only once. Tokens don't expire, and their access is controlled only by the role. There are no separate scopes. Roles A token with its own identity uses the role you pick when you create it. You can change the role later with Edit . Older tokens that have no role act as Admin. A token that acts as a user or bot has no role of its own. It always uses that user's current role, so changing the user's role changes what the token can do. See Roles and user management for what each role allows. Who actions are attributed to Token with its own identity: actions show up under the token's name and icon. Token that acts as a user or bot: actions are attributed to that user or bot. Bots Bots are identities for automation, so API activity is attributed to the bot instead of to a teammate. Bots can't sign in to Pylon. To create one, go to Settings > Workspace > Users , open the Bots tab, and click New Bot . Give it a name, an avatar, and a role. Then select the bot under Act as user or bot when you create a token. IP allowlist Add IP addresses (for example 203.0.113.10 ) or CIDR blocks (for example 203.0.113.0/24 ) to restrict where the token can be used. You can add up to 20 entries. If the list is empty, the token works from any IP. Pylon checks the public IP address your requests come from, so add the public egress IPs or ranges of the servers that call the API. Private addresses such as 10.0.0.0/8 or 192.168.0.0/16 never match. A request from an address that isn't on the list returns 401 with the invalid_api_token error code. Manage tokens The Tokens tab shows each token's Acts as , Token preview , Role , Created by , Last used , and Created values. From the … menu on a token you can: Edit: change the name, role, or IP allowlist. Duplicate Token: create a new token with the same settings. Rotate: generate a new token value. The current token stops working immediately. Delete: permanently revoke the token. Calls using it stop working immediately. View Activity: open the token's request logs. Review API request logs Only Admins can view request logs. Go to Settings > Integrations & dev > API and open the Logs tab, or choose View Activity from a token's … menu to see only that token's requests. Filter by token, or choose All tokens , and by a date range of up to 90 days. The range defaults to the last 7 days. Each request shows when it was made, the token, who it acted as, the method, endpoint, response status, source IP, user agent, and request ID. Requests made with a token that was since deleted still appear. Requests rejected for authentication or rate limits aren't logged, and older requests may not show a token. When tokens are revoked automatically When a user is deactivated, Pylon deletes: every API token that user created, and every API token that acts as that user. Before you deactivate someone who created tokens your integrations rely on, create replacement tokens from another Admin's account. An Admin who has created Admin-role tokens can't be moved to a different role until those tokens are deleted. Previous API Next API conventions Last updated 26 days ago Was this helpful? access for Pylon support — — ✓ Frequently asked questions How is Pylon priced? Pylon is priced based on the number of seats and the number of agentic credits your team needs. Because B2B support teams vary significantly in size and workflow, pricing reflects your team's unique needs. Book a demo and we'll put together a quote specific to your setup. Is pricing per seat, per ticket, or per account? Pylon's pricing is seat-based and credit usage-based. You're not charged per ticket, so your costs stay predictable as your customer base grows, even as ticket volume scales. What's included in every plan? Every plan includes core ticketing, unified ticketing (Slack, email, and chat widget), omnichannel support, a knowledge base, NPS and CSAT surveys, and analytics. Are AI features included, or are they a separate add-on? Pylon's agentic features (including the Assist Agent, Automations, Support Agent, and Slack Agent) are accessible when you purchase credits, not sold as separate add-ons. Does Pylon offer annual and monthly billing, and is there a discount for paying annually? Pylon offers both annual and monthly billing. When you commit to credits upfront, you will receive a discount. Do I have to buy credits upfront? No. Pylon offers both pay-as-you-go credits and committed credit plans, so teams can buy credits as they need them or commit upfront. You can purchase additional credits in-product anytime. Is there a minimum seat requirement or minimum contract size? There is a minimum seat count for new customers. Pylon is built for B2B support teams rather than solo operators, so it's designed to deliver value at team scale. What does a contract with Pylon look like? Standard contracts are annual. Multi-year agreements are available for teams that want rate lock and additional flexibility. Credits can be used across the entire contract term and buying more at once will result in a higher credit discount. What counts as a "seat"? A seat covers any teammate who needs to work tickets, including agents and admins with inbox access. Stakeholders who only need visibility into conversations, without working them, can use a viewer seat. Do you have viewer seats? Yes, Pylon has view-only seats. Your sales representative will work with you on the number of viewer seats your team needs. Does Pylon offer a free trial or free plan? Pylon offers free trials for prospects. Your sales representative will work with you on setting up the demo organization. Is there a minimum number of accounts required for Account Intelligence? Yes. Account Intelligence requires a minimum of 50 customer accounts. The platform that fits exactly what your team needs. Join 1,800+ B2B companies who have left legacy platforms behind. Thank you! https://help.plain.com/article/does-the-.text: AI Agents - Does the Plain MCP server support API key authentication? | Help Center Skip to content ⌘ K Inbox Ask a human Ask an AI agent How can I help you? This conversation will be visible to Plain employees Home / AI Agents Does the Plain MCP server support API key authentication? Updated 2 Sep 2026 by Plain Copy How authentication works Use a custom MCP server with a machine user API key Related documentation No. The Plain Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at https://mcp.plain.com/mcp supports OAuth only. How authentication works You authenticate with your existing Plain account through OAuth. The MCP session inherits your permissions, and replies and actions appear under your user, as in the app. This ties MCP activity to a real user for audit and attribution. Each person who uses the server needs a Plain account with any role, including Viewer, and must complete the OAuth flow once in their MCP client, such as Cursor, Claude or ChatGPT. There is no shared credential that lets several engineers connect. Use a custom MCP server with a machine user API key To give a team of engineers access to Plain data without individual Viewer accounts, build a lightweight custom MCP server that wraps Plain's GraphQL API with a single machine user API key. In Settings, open Machine Users and create a machine user with read-only permissions. Generate an API key for that machine user. Build an MCP server that uses the key to call Plain's GraphQL API and exposes the tools your team needs. Point your engineers' MCP clients at your custom server. The trade-off is that all activity goes through the machine user, so there is no per-engineer attribution in your workspace timeline. This conversation will be visible to Plain employees Home Plain plans and pricing Updated 27 Oct 2026 by Youmna Copy Plans Foundation Horizon Frontier Prices and included credits Plain has three plans: Foundation, Horizon and Frontier. Each plan charges a price for every member seat , the seat a user needs to reply to customers, and includes a monthly allowance of credits for your workspace. Full details are on the pricing page . Viewer seats are free and unlimited on every plan, so you can invite your entire team to Plain to increase visibility on questions from customers. Every plan starts with a free trial lasting 7 days, and the trial doesn't need a credit card. Plans Each plan suits a different size of support team, and each one includes everything in the plan before it. The lists below highlight some of the features in each plan, not all of them. Foundation Foundation is for companies at an early stage. It supports up to 5 member seats and includes, among other features: 25 Slack channels and 2 email addresses 1 Help Center, with a knowledge base, Ask AI, and a customer inbox A headless support portal Horizon Horizon is for companies with a dedicated Support or Success function. It supports 3 to 10 member seats and includes everything in Foundation, plus, among other features: Unlimited Slack channels, up to 10 email addresses, and unlimited Help Centers Microsoft Teams Advanced workflow rules, business hours, and SLAs Team reporting and suggested responses Frontier Frontier is for large support organizations and enterprise teams. It supports 10 or more member seats and includes everything in Horizon, plus, among other features: Pricing based on volume of seats, or organization wide pricing Up to 25 email addresses External Agents, so you can bring your own agent to Plain Concierge onboarding Prices and included credits Plain's pricing has two components: seats and credits. You pay for each member seat on your team, and your plan includes a monthly allowance of credits for your workspace's usage based features, such as the Customer Agent and the Sidekick Agent . The included allowance is designed to help you get started with them. Seat prices are per member seat per month. Included credits go to the whole workspace each month, including on annual plans, and reset on your billing anniversary. For what each action costs, see How credits work . Plan Billing Seat price Included credits per month Member seats Foundation Monthly $55 1,000 Up to 5 Foundation Annual $45 1,000 Up to 5 Horizon Monthly $139 2,500 3 to 10 Horizon Annual $99 2,500 3 to 10 Frontier Annual Custom Custom 10 or more Frontier is available on annual billing only. For Frontier pricing, email sales@plain.com . If your workspace needs more credits than its plan includes, you can buy top up credits or increase your monthly allowance. To learn more about how credits work, head over to our docs . This conversation will be visible to Plain employees Home / Developer & API Migrating to accounts with the Plain API Updated 4 Nov 2026 by Juan Copy What an account is Fields Operations Permissions Webhooks Customer cards Configuration Compatibility Accounts replace companies in the Plain API, and they are the new name for tenants. This article lists the GraphQL fields, operations, permissions, webhooks, and customer card request to update in your integration. For the steps inside your workspace, see Migrating companies and tenants to accounts . The product UI switches its labels from tenants to accounts between October 26 and November 1, 2026. What an account is An account is the organization a customer belongs to. A customer can belong to more than one account. Read those memberships from accountMemberships on the customer. See Accounts in the docs. Each account record includes: name externalId primaryDomain and alternateDomains accountFields logoUrl In GraphQL, source is API , SALESFORCE , HUBSPOT , ATTIO , or EMAIL_DOMAIN . Webhook payloads use api , salesforce , hubspot , attio , or email_domain . Store a company account owner in a user reference account field. The field type is USER_REFERENCE_TYPE . Tiers and their SLAs apply to an account. Set the tier with updateAccountTier . HubSpot, Salesforce, and Attio map a CRM company to an account and a company attribute to an account field. See CRM . Fields Account inputs add accountIdentifier , accountIdentifiers , accountId , accountIds , and accountFields . Plain marks the tenant and company fields they replace as deprecated, and those fields still work. Send one name per field in a request, not both. Use Instead of accountIdentifier tenantIdentifier , companyIdentifier accountIdentifiers tenantIdentifiers , companyIdentifiers accountId tenantId , companyId accountIds tenantIds , companyIds accountFields tenantFields account tenant , company accounts tenants , companies on a saved view hasAccounts hasCompany , hasTenants hasAccountFieldExternalIds hasTenantFieldExternalIds accountMemberships tenantMemberships , and company on a customer accountMembershipPolicy tenantMembershipPolicy customerAccounts customerCompany , customerTenants These inputs accept the new fields: CreateThreadInput and CreateThreadFromSlackMessageInput accept accountIdentifier . UpsertCustomerOnCreateInput accepts accountIdentifiers . ThreadsFilter , CustomersFilter , and ThreadMetricFilters accept accountIdentifiers . ThreadsFilter and ThreadMetricFilters also accept accountFields . CreateTaskInput , UpdateTaskInput , and TierMemberIdentifierInput accept accountId . TasksFilter , ThreadClustersFilter , ThreadLinkGroupFilter , and BroadcastAudienceFilterInput accept accountIds . SavedThreadsViewFilterInput accepts accounts and accountFields . ThreadsDisplayOptionsInput accepts hasAccounts and hasAccountFieldExternalIds . Thread exposes account . ThreadChannelAssociation exposes accountId and accountMembershipPolicy . Help center access settings accept accountIds . Portal thread visibility accepts customerAccounts and overrideCustomerAccounts . Grouping and access enums use ACCOUNT where they used COMPANY or TENANT : ThreadsGroupBy and ThreadMetricGroupBy use ACCOUNT . ThreadMetricGroupBy.ACCOUNT_FIELD replaces TENANT_FIELD and needs subKey set to the field's external ID. DiscussionSourceEntityType and ThreadScopePrimitiveType use ACCOUNT . ThreadScopePrimitiveType is the dimension on a custom role access filter. Operations Call the account operation. Plain marks the tenant and company operations as deprecated, and each deprecation reason names the account operation. Account operation Replaces accounts tenants , companies account tenant , company searchAccounts searchTenants , searchCompanies accountFieldSchemas tenantFieldSchemas createAccount createTenant upsertAccount upsertTenant , upsertCompany deleteAccount deleteTenant , deleteCompany addCustomerToAccounts addCustomerToTenants removeCustomerFromAccounts removeCustomerFromTenants setCustomerAccounts setCustomerTenants , updateCustomerCompany updateAccountTier updateTenantTier , updateCompanyTier importAccounts importTenants updateThreadAccount updateThreadTenant upsertAccountField upsertTenantField upsertAccountFieldSchema upsertTenantFieldSchema deleteAccountField deleteTenantField deleteAccountFieldSchema deleteTenantFieldSchema importAccountFieldSchemas importTenantFieldSchemas importAccountFieldSchemasFromService importTenantFieldSchemasFromService setupAccountFieldSchemaMapping setupTenantFieldSchemaMapping removeAccountFieldSchemaMapping removeTenantFieldSchemaMapping updateThreadChannelAssociationAccountMembershipPolicy updateThreadChannelAssociationTenantMembershipPolicy The @team-plain/graphql SDK exposes upsertAccount on client.mutation . upsertTenant and upsertCompany are deprecated and point at upsertAccount . The current calls are documented under Accounts in the API docs. Permissions Account calls use tenant permission strings. accounts , account , and searchAccounts need tenant:read . createAccount needs tenant:create . upsertAccount needs tenant:create and tenant:edit . deleteAccount needs tenant:delete . Account field calls use tenantField and tenantFieldSchema strings. deleteAccountField needs tenant:edit . Adding or removing a customer needs customer:edit plus customerTenantMembership:create or customerTenantMembership:delete . Account fields lists the field strings for each call. The companies , company , and searchCompanies queries need company:read . upsertCompany needs company:create and company:edit . deleteCompany needs company:delete . The API docs page for each account call lists the strings it needs. Webhooks Account events ship in webhook version 2026-10-06 and later. A target on an earlier version, including an unversioned target, does not receive them. Move the target to 2026-10-06 or later. The events are: account.account_created account.account_updated account.account_deleted account.account_membership_changed account.account_field_created account.account_field_updated account.account_field_deleted thread.thread_tenant_updated keeps its event type. The payload includes tenant and previousTenant . Customer cards The unversioned customer card request has no version field. It sends the account under tenant , with id and externalId . Request format 2026-10-19 sets version to "2026-10-19" and sends that same object under account . The full request is in request versions . Update your customer card API so it reads account when version is 2026-10-19 . Go to Settings > Customer cards and set Request format to 2026-10-19 . The setting applies to every customer card in the workspace. You can switch back to unversioned if your API needs more time. Changing the format reloads every card the next time it is viewed. Plain doesn't reuse cards cached under the other format. Configuration Saved views, workflows, custom role access filters, and help center access lists that reference a company show an "Accounts are replacing companies" hint. Plain converts them to the matching account settings. Replace an Assign to company account owner workflow step with Assign to user , and select a user reference account field. Compatibility Deprecated tenant and company fields and operations still work. The deprecation reason on each one names the account field or operation to call. Move your integration to those names. Yes — additional Inboxes beyond the number included in your plan are available for $10 per month when paid annually (or $12 per month). Additional Docs sites are available for $20 per month when paid annually (or $24 per month). The Free plan is limited to just 1 Inbox and 1 Docs site. What counts as an AI resolution? A resolution is a single conversation that is resolved by Envoy's built-in AI agent, Scout, without human assistance. A resolution is counted only if the customer receives an AI response and doesn’t use escalation, search the knowledge base, ask more questions, or indicate that they need more help. If a customer requests more help with natural language or by selecting the “I still need help” button, the conversation won’t count as a resolution and you won’t be charged. You'll only be charged for one resolution per conversation, even if Scout responds to multiple questions. Can I set caps on AI resolution spending? Yes — you can set a monthly cap on Envoy resolutions. If you hit your spending cap, your AI agent will be disabled automatically for the remainder of the monthly cycle. You’ll receive email notifications as you get closer to your cap. This option allows for predictable billing, so you’ll never be surprised at the end of the month. How does the free trial work? For some annual payments, wire or ACH transfer is also available. Free accounts don’t need to add a payment method. Do you offer discounts for startups or non-profits? If you plan to build a public app you have to use OAuth2. Each access token (or API key) is tied to a specific user and has the same permissions as the user that holds them. Requests made with an access token will act on behalf of a user and will have access to the resources their permissions allow. As an admin, you can easily generate and revoke your access token in the settings of your account. Example: If you use an Access Token for a user with an Observer Agent role, then you can only do the things that an Observer agent can. Learn more about roles here . How do I get my API key? Log in to your Gorgias account Navigate to Settings → REST API Click the Create API key button Once you have your credentials, you can start performing requests directly from the API documentation . Request example cURL curl --request GET \ --url https://your-customer-account.gorgias.com/api/account \ --header 'Authorization: Basic base64encode(USERNAME:API_KEY)' 👉 Since we're using HTTP Basic Authentication , the USERNAME:API_KEY pair has to be a base64 encoded string. Note the : between the USERNAME and API_KEY is a separator used to differentiate between the username and the password. Introducing the Gladly API At Gladly, we believe that customer service is best when it's a conversation. That means more than just helping customers with one-off questions or issues: it's about making them feel known, valued, and respected for the individuals they are. The Gladly API was built to help facilitate those relationships, providing agents with the rich customer context they need to deliver seamless experiences that make customers feel like they're more than just a number in a sea of others. Overview You can integrate easily with Gladly by calling Gladly's REST API and implementing the Lookup API to provide data from your own services. Some examples of what you do through Gladly APIs include managing customer profile data, interacting with a customer's timeline, providing the latest information about a customer's orders, and more. REST API Clients can access the REST API via HTTPS at your organization's Gladly domain (e.g. https://{organization}.gladly.com ). Resources follow REST semantics and utilize industry-standard HTTP verbs, response codes, and authentication schemes. In addition, all responses and payloads are in JSON with consistent error codes and formats. Lookup API The Gladly Lookup API allows your organization to provide data services to power the agent's experience with a complete view of your customers' information, transactions, and activity. You can provide a web service that implements the Lookup API and Gladly will call it when that data is needed. Like the REST API, the Lookup API is specified using REST semantics, and exchanges JSON requests and responses authenticated and signed with secure keys. Gladly will perform lookups when certain activities occur within Gladly, such as when a customer's profile is loaded. A detailed overview of Lookup Adaptor architecture, requests, resposnes and more can be found here . Testing Test the myriad possibilities of the Gladly API in a safe, secure space. We'll enable the Gladly API in a separate sandbox environment, so you can experiment freely without impacting your production environment (or vice versa). Your sandbox environment is accessible at https://{organization}.gladly.qa , where organization is your company name. For specific API endpoints, see documentation below. Getting Started Think of this section as getting the keys to unlocking your access to the Gladly APIs. First, you'll need to set up an account with the necessary API permissions . With these permissions, you can then go on to create the API Token(s) you need to access Gladly's API resources . Permissions Gladly Administrators can set API permissions on an agent-by-agent basis. We'll discuss how this maps to API access in the section on authentication below. To allow a user to create API tokens and access the API: Log in to your Gladly instance. Open the menu on the top left-hand corner of the page. Navigate to Settings > *Users Search and click the user profile you wish to give access to. You'll see a permission called API User . Select it, while making sure to keep the user's Agent role intact. Hit Save to give access. We recommend creating a dedicated user to make API calls, whose account won't be used for agent and organization management. This will help you with any future audits of API activity vs. agent activity. Creating API Tokens You must create an API token to access Gladly API resources (see above Permissions ). If your profile already has access to the API User permission, you'll see a menu item titled More settings . Click More settings : Click API Tokens , then the Create Token button on the upper right-hand corner of the page: A token will be generated and named, by default, New Token (though depending on whether you have existing tokens, it may be named New Token 2, or New Token 3, etc.). You can rename the token to something more easily referenceable by clicking the name to edit. This token will be associated with your agent profile, which we refer to as the API User in this document. For security purposes, you'll only see a new token once before you navigate away from the page. Replacing/Rotating API Tokens Should you lose this token, or wish to rotate your application keys, you can do the following: Generate a new token. Store the new token in a secure location. Delete the old token. Update your applications/scripts with the new token. Authentication BasicAuth Gladly API uses token-based Basic Authentication . API tokens are associated with designated Gladly users. To create and use an API token, your user must have the API User permission. An API token can be used to perform any API request without restriction. user name password agent email API token The credentials must be passed via an Authorization HTTP header. All requests must be made over HTTPS. curl -u user@organization.com: $GLADLY_API_TOKEN \ https://organization.gladly.com/api/v1/organization Security Scheme Type HTTP HTTP Authorization Scheme basic Agents An Agent represents the user profile of a person who helps customers in Gladly. The API allows you to lookup Agents who participated in conversations with customers. List Agents Returns a list of agents. Responses 200 Agents get /api/v1/agents https://organization.gladly.com /api/v1/agents Response samples 200 Content type application/json Copy Expand all Collapse all [ { "id" : "WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA" , "name" : "Amy Agent" , "emailAddress" : "amy.agent@company.com" } ] Get Agent Get an agent profile by their unique id. path Parameters agentId required string Example: WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA id of the agent Responses 200 Agent get /api/v1/agents/{agentId} https://organization.gladly.com /api/v1/agents/{agentId} Response samples 200 Content type application/json Copy Expand all Collapse all { "id" : "WmeA3Y51Q5ayCAaZ1AotIA" , "name" : "Amy Agent" , "emailAddress" : "amy.agent@company.com" } Get Agent Availability Get an agent's availability. The Public Answers API allows you to search and retrieve Public Answers (created directly in the Gladly UI), which you can display in the Chat web widget, use to build your website's help center/FAQ page, or publish on any page on your website. This API can be used without an API token because it only provides access to public content. You may also work with Gladly Support to enable CORS access so the API can be used directly from client-side javascript. How a user creates a public answer in Gladly How that answer is searched and displayed on the Chat Web widget Search public answers Returns a list of answers that match the provided query string. path Parameters orgId required string Example: ihKsWxiZCDVtXg1iwVmT9Q id of your organization You can look up the ID using the Get organization API. query Parameters q string Example: q=reset%20password search term lng string Example: lng=en-us language code audienceId string Example: audienceId=en-us Audience ID. The Audience ID can be retrieved by going to Settings > Audiences in Gladly, then clicking on the Edit button next to the Audience in question. The ID will be in the page URL. Conversations API enables you to interact with the customer conversation timeline. Error Handling Conversations can be merged into one another when their customers are merged. An endpoint that resolves a conversation or customer id which was merged away does not return 404 ; it reports the surviving id in meta.new of a moved error. GET /api/v1/conversations/{conversationId} returns 301 with a Location header, so clients that follow redirects transparently receive the surviving conversation. The other endpoints that resolve a merged id return 410 Gone with no Location header; reissue the request against the id in meta.new . Each operation lists 410 among its responses where this applies. Endpoints addressed by a conversation item id, and those that list conversations for a customer, do not resolve the merged id and are unaffected. With the right tools and best practices, you’ll have a secure, smooth authentication flow. Whether you’re handling OAuth 2.0 , verifying requests , or setting up Sign in with Slack , we’ve got you covered. Authentication basics ​ Before your app can access Slack data or interact with Slack workspaces, it must go through an authentication process. This involves obtaining the necessary tokens and permissions for your app to function properly. Slack apps use OAuth scopes to govern what they can access. These are added in the app settings when building an app. You will attach these scopes to your tokens. Check out tokens to learn more. You can rotate those tokens too! Find out how on the Using token rotation page. Key concepts ​ OAuth 2.0 : Learn how to use OAuth 2.0 to securely authenticate users and request access tokens. Tokens : Understand the different types of tokens your app can use (user tokens, bot tokens, and app tokens) and how to manage them, as well as employ token rotation and expiry to keep things fresh. Security best practices : Learn about security practices for managing authentication, such as validating tokens, handling sensitive data, and protecting your app from unauthorized access. Reference ​ Scopes and Permissions : Find the right permissions for your app to ensure access is limited to only the necessary data. https://docs.slack.dev/app-management/qu.text: Creating an app from app settings | Slack Developer Docs guide Skip to main content Guides Reference Samples Tools Changelog Dev Program MANAGE APPS Quickstart Resources Slack platform concepts AI in Slack APIs App management Creating an app from app settings Distribution Hosting Slack apps Onboarding users to your app App manifests Admin resources Authentication Block Kit Enterprise Enterprise Search for apps GovSlack Interactivity Messaging Slack Marketplace Surfaces Workflows Legacy 日本語のドキュメント App management Creating an app from app settings Copy as markdown On this page Creating an app from app settings In the following guide, you'll create a basic Slack app that can send messages using webhooks. Want a step-by-step guide using the Slack CLI and Bolt framework? Head over to this Quickstart guide. 1. Creating an app ​ Create a Slack app via the apps page by selecting the following button: Create new app (opens in new tab) Click Create New App . Select Pick features , then click Continue . Enter your App Name . For this example, enter "Grocery Reminders". Select the Workspace where you'll be developing your app. You'll be able to distribute your app to other workspaces later if you choose. Click Continue until you reach the Review your app page, then click Create . If a pop-up appears letting you know your app can't do anything yet until you add scopes, click Create Anyway . tip If you need to update the name of your app later, you can do so from your app's Home tab . Changing the app name entry under Basic Information will update the bot name rather than the app name; this is the name that appears when the app performs actions such as posting in a channel or sending a direct message. 2. Requesting scopes ​ Next, you'll need to request scopes for your app. Scopes give your app permission to perform actions, such as posting messages in your workspace. Slack apps can't post to any public channel by default; they gain that ability by asking for permission explicitly with the use of scopes. Request the chat:write.public scope to gain the ability to post in all public channels without joining. Otherwise, you'll need to use the conversations.join scope, or have your app invited into a channel by a user before it can post. Within OAuth & Permissions , scroll down to Scopes . Under Bot Token Scopes , select Add an OAuth Scope . To allow your app to post messages, add the chat:write scope. To allow your app to access public Slack channels, add the channels:read scope. In general, you'll add scopes to your bot token, not your user token. A notable exception is if you need to act as a specific user (for example, posting messages on behalf of a user, or setting a user's status). Slack apps cannot access the Real Time Messaging (RTM) API The Events API allows your app to listen to Slack events in a structured, safe way. If you require access to RTM (for example, because you're building your app behind a corporate firewall), you'll need to create a legacy Slack app and use its bot token to call rtm.connect . For more information, refer to Legacy: Real Time Message API . 3. Installing and authorizing the app ​ Scroll back to the top of the OAuth & Permissions page. Install your app by selecting the Install to Workspace button. You'll now be sent through the Slack OAuth flow. Select Allow on the following screen. When you follow this flow, you're playing the part of the installing user , not the app. If you were adding your app to a different workspace besides your own, this flow would be completed by a user from that workspace instead of you. After installation, navigate back to the OAuth & Permissions page. You'll see an access token under OAuth Tokens . Access tokens represent the permissions delegated to your app by the installing user. Keep it secret. Keep it safe. At a minimum, avoid checking them into public version control. Instead, access them via an environment variable. Your access token allows you to call the methods described by the scopes you requested. For example, your chat:write scope allows your app to post messages. Your app isn't a member of any channels yet, so pick a channel to add some test messages in and /invite your app as in the following example slash command: /invite @Grocery Reminders You'll see a message posted in the channel confirming that your app was added. 4. Configuring the app for event listening ​ Slack apps listen and respond to events. We've already touched on one way an app can respond: by calling chat.postMessage to post a message. Apps can also respond to events such as mentions in a channel, menu selections, or users sending the app a direct message. Apps listen with the Events API . Let's subscribe to the app_mention event. Select Event Subscriptions and toggle Enable Events to ON. Within Subscribe to bot events , select Add Bot User Event , then search for app_mention . As with scopes, always subscribe to events with a bot user . If your app will be using HTTP Request URLs, set the Request URL to a URL where your app's server listens to the incoming HTTP requests. Slack will send an HTTP request there when your app is mentioned, allowing your app to determine how it will respond. Note that you'll need to implement your own server for this step, as well as to send messages with webhooks. You may want to explore the Bolt family of SDKs , which can allow you to implement a server that listens for events automatically. Also note that this step is not required if your app is set up to use Socket Mode; refer to comparing HTTP & Socket Mode for more details. You'll notice that the app_mention event requires the app_mentions:read scope. Events are like API methods: they allow your app access to information in Slack, so you'll need permissions for them. Reinstall your app to the workspace with this new scope. Now you'll be notified when your app is mentioned, and can determine how your app will respond. 5. Sending a message with a webhook ​ Select Incoming Webhooks from the left sidebar and toggle Activate Incoming Webhooks to ON. Select Add New Webhook to Workspace to start the webhook flow. Select the channel you previously invited your app to and then Allow on the following screen. Reinstall your app to the workspace with this new feature by selecting the Reinstall to Workspace button within the Install App page in the left sidebar. Navigate back to Incoming Webhooks and view the new entry listed under WebHook URLs for Your Workspace . Copy your webhook. Create a new HTTP POST request with the webhook as follows: POST https://hooks.slack.com/services/EXAMPLE/REDACTED/WEBHOOK Content-type: application/json { "text": "Gotta get the bread and milk!" } Navigate to the channel your app was installed in to see the message posted by your app: Oslo Gotta get the bread and milk! Onward ​ Congratulations on creating your very own Slack app! Keep learning about all the things your app can do by checking out the following: Sending messages using Incoming Webhooks Designing Slack apps App interactivity overview Building with Block Kit Previous Overview Next Distribution Copy as markdown 1. Creating an app 2. Requesting scopes 3. Installing and authorizing the app 4. Configuring the app for event listening 5. Sending a message with a webhook Onward . Workspace admins can approve and manage all MCP client integrations, keeping your Slack data safe. This guide discusses the MCP server offerings from Slack and how to develop with the Slack MCP server. Slack MCP server features ​ The Slack MCP server provides tools for searching through Slack, retrieving and sending messages, managing canvases, managing users, uploading files, and working with lists. Each of these tools provides useful functionality for interacting with Slack; combine them for comprehensive integrations that grasp your team's context and history. Searching throughout Slack ​ The MCP server can search for a variety of information found throughout a Slack workspace: Messages and files — filter by date, user, and content type. Retrieve metadata and content. Users in a workspace — filter by name (with partial name matching), email, and user ID. Retrieve user details and statuses. Private and public channels — filter by channel name and description. Retrieve channel metadata. List user channels — list the channels you're a member of, filterable by type (public, private, DMs, group DMs), name prefix, and workspace. Supports pagination and can return full details, names only, or IDs only. Archived channels are included by default. Emoji — returns the list of custom emoji available in the workspace. Retrieving and sending messages ​ The MCP server can retrieve and send messages throughout a Slack workspace: Send messages — send messages to any type of conversation in Slack. Schedule messages — schedule a message to be sent to a conversation at a future time. Draft messages — draft, format, and preview messages directly within AI clients. Read channels — grab the complete message history of channels. Read threads — grab complete message thread conversations. Create a conversation/channel — creates a new Slack channel, group DM, or IM conversation on behalf of the authenticated user. Add reactions — adds an emoji reaction to a Slack message on behalf of the authenticated user. Get reactions — retrieve the emoji reactions on a Slack message. Managing canvases ​ The MCP server can interact and modify Slack canvases: Create/update a canvas — create and share rich, formatted documents. Read a canvas — export canvases as markdown files. Managing users ​ Fetch user info — access complete user profile info, including custom profile fields and statuses. List channel members — retrieve a list of user IDs for members of a given Slack channel or conversation. Managing files ​ Upload files — upload files to Slack via a two-step process. The file isn't visible until the second step completes. Call the slack_get_file_upload_url tool to get a signed upload URL and file ID, then POST your file bytes to that URL. Call the slack_complete_file_upload tool with the file ID to finalize it, optionally sharing the file to a channel with a message. Working with lists ​ The MCP server can work with Slack lists, which hold structured tabular data with typed columns (text, date, select, user, and more): Create and read lists — create lists with custom schemas and read their contents. Update lists and records — update list metadata and columns, and add or update individual records (rows). Columns are addressed by display name or internal key. Column types include select/multi_select with color-coded options. Example use cases ​ There are many possibilities with the Slack MCP server. Here are just a few ideas: Create an AI assistant in Slack that can search through your team's Slack history to answer questions, find past decisions, and provide context for current projects. Bring content from outside Slack into Slack via messages and canvases for discussion with coworkers. Bring content from Slack to AI agents, providing them full context of projects that exist across multiple products. Rate limits ​ Like all Slack Web API methods, the Slack MCP server is subject to rate limits. Limits are enforced per tool or action type. Whether an action is performed via an MCP tool or directly through Slack Web API methods, the same rate limits apply. Here is the full list of MCP tools and their associated rate limit: MCP Tool Rate Limit Search messages & files Special rate limits apply; consult method page documentation Read files Tier 4: 100+ per minute Search emoji Tier 2: 20+ per minute Search users Tier 2: 20+ per minute Search channels Tier 2: 20+ per minute Send message Special rate limits apply; consult method page documentation Schedule message Tier 3: 50+ per minute Read a channel Tier 3: 50+ per minute Read a thread Tier 3: 50+ per minute Create conversation/channel Tier 2: 20+ per minute Add reactions Tier 3: 50+ per minute Get reactions Tier 3: 50+ per minute Create a canvas Tier 2: 20+ per minute Update a canvas Tier 3: 50+ per minute Read a canvas Tier 3: 50+ per minute / Tier 4: 100+ per minute Read a user profile Tier 4: 100+ per minute List channel members Tier 4: 100+ per minute List user channels Tier 2: 20+ per minute Upload a file Tier 4: 100+ per minute Create/read/update a list Tier 2: 20+ per minute / Tier 3: 50+ per minute Transport protocol and endpoint ​ Slack supports JSON-RPC 2.0 over Streamable HTTP. All requests should be sent to: https://mcp.slack.com/mcp We do not support SSE-based connections or Dynamic Client Registration at this time. App Identity ​ MCP clients must be backed by a registered Slack app with a fixed app ID and hardcode that app ID. This allows Slack to: Let admins manage and approve your app/MCP client app using standard Slack app approval process. Associate requests with your app for logging, rate limits, and access control. Provide better support and visibility into usage. If you're already using a Slack app for your integration, you can reuse it for MCP access. Only directory-published apps or internal apps may use MCP. Security concerns ​ When using the Slack MCP server, please be mindful about connecting to or utilizing other MCP servers at the same time. Different servers may have their own security, stability, and usage characteristics, so think carefully before mixing them together. Use judgment when evaluating what to connect and share across environments. Using these clients means giving them access to your Slack data so you can use it as context while interacting with those apps. Audit MCP activity with the associated audit logs . Only apps published in the Slack Marketplace and internal apps can use MCP at this time; unlisted apps are prohibited from using MCP. IP allowlist ​ If your app has allowed IP address ranges configured, requests to the Slack MCP server are subject to the same restrictions. API calls originating from IP addresses not on your allowlist will be rejected. Ensure that the IP addresses your MCP client uses are included in your app's allowed list. Authentication and Token Handling ​ Slack supports confidential OAuth for MCP clients. You'll need to use your app's client_id and client_secret for Slack OAuth. If your MCP client supports OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) per MCP spec, you can rely on that. Users go through OAuth consent and authorize the app. You can initiate this OAuth request from your UX following standard MCP metadata discovery files: https://mcp.slack.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource https://mcp.slack.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server OAuth URL and endpoints ​ Authorization endpoint for Slack user tokens: https://slack.com/oauth/v2_user/authorize Token endpoint for Slack user tokens: https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.user.access (method docs here ) If you also want to generate bot tokens (for in-Slack experience), follow instructions here . PKCE support is now available! Read more here . Using the Slack MCP server with partner apps ​ If you'd rather not build a Slack app, you can use the Slack MCP server through a partner-built client, no coding needed. For the current list of partner apps and how to connect them, see the Guide to MCP in Slack in the Slack Help Center. The Real Time Search (RTS) API offers access to Slack data via API call. Ways to make requests to the Twilio APIs ways-to-make-requests-to-the-twilio-apis page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback You can make an HTTP request to the Twilio API in the following ways: Make a raw HTTP request either in your code (for example, by using a module like got in NodeJS (link takes you to an external page) ) or with a tool like Postman (link takes you to an external page) . Use a Twilio SDK for your preferred programming language. Use the Twilio CLI if you prefer working in the terminal. Authentication authentication page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback (information) Environment variables Always store your credentials in environment variables before sharing any code or deploying to production. Learn more about setting environment variables (link takes you to an external page) . To authenticate requests to the Twilio APIs, use HTTP Basic authentication (link takes you to an external page) . Use your API key SID as the username and your API key secret as the password. (information) Regional API credentials Twilio API credentials are region-specific resources. If your account uses Twilio Regions , see Manage Regional API credentials . Use API keys use-api-keys page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback An API key is a unique identifier that allows a client to access your Twilio account and create, read, update, or delete resources through the Twilio APIs. You can create multiple API keys for different purposes, such as for different developers or subsystems within your application. If a key is compromised or no longer used, you can revoke it to prevent unauthorized access. Use API keys for your applications unless the API reference or guide specifies Account SID and Auth Token authentication . If a key is compromised or no longer used, revoke it to prevent unauthorized access without affecting your other applications. You can create an API key either in the Twilio Console or using the API . The API key types are Main , Standard , and Restricted (Key resource v1 only). The following table describes each type: Key type Access permissions Create in Console Create with REST API Main Full access to all Twilio API resources. Equivalent to using your Account SID and Auth Token for API requests. Yes No Standard Access to all Twilio API resources, except for Accounts ( /Accounts ) or Keys ( /Accounts/{SID}/Keys , /v1/Keys ) resources. Yes Yes Restricted Customized, fine-grained access to specific Twilio API resources. Learn more about Restricted API keys . Yes Yes ( v1 only ) When making an API request, use your API key as the username and your API key secret as the password. Note : In the following example, you must use a Main API key. List accounts Link to code sample: List accounts curl Report code block Copy code block 1 curl -X GET "https://api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts.json?PageSize=20" \ 2 -u $TWILIO_API_KEY : $TWILIO_API_SECRET The user remains logged in for the duration of the request. Learn more about how Twilio handles authentication . Use your Account SID and Auth Token using-your-account-sid-and-auth-token page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback When an API reference or guide specifies Account SID and Auth Token authentication, use the Account SID as the HTTP Basic authentication username and the Auth Token as the password. Store these values in the TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID and TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN environment variables. Follow the credential requirements for the operation you're performing: Accounts examples use Account SID and Auth Token authentication. For subaccount management , use the parent account's credentials. Main API keys are an alternative, but Standard API keys can't access Accounts resources. Auth Token promotion and Secondary Auth Token examples use Account SID and Auth Token authentication for token rotation. Test credential examples use your test Account SID and test Auth Token, not your live credentials or an API key. Guides such as A2P 10DLC onboarding for ISVs and the BrandRegistrations API reference specify which account's credentials to use. Don't substitute parent account credentials for subaccount credentials unless the guide supports that operation. For example, the following request lists accounts using Account SID and Auth Token authentication: List accounts with an Auth Token Link to code sample: List accounts with an Auth Token curl Report code block Copy code block 1 curl -X GET "https://api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts.json?PageSize=20" \ 2 -u $TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID : $TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN Twilio SDKs twilio-sdks page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback A Twilio SDK is a server-side SDK that helps you use Twilio's REST APIs, generate TwiML, and perform other common server-side programming tasks. Twilio SDKs can handle credential management and simplify the authentication process. All Twilio SDKs come with a Utilities class that validates requests by passing your credentials to the library. HTTP methods for API interactions http-methods-for-api-interactions page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Twilio APIs use standard RESTful HTTP methods to perform actions on resources. The following examples demonstrate the most common methods: POST : Create or update a resource. GET : Retrieve a resource. DELETE : Delete a resource. Using an unsupported content type might cause unexpected behavior or errors. Global Edge Locations and network entry global-edge-locations-and-network-entry page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Twilio global infrastructure allows you to optimize request routing for better performance. You can specify which Twilio network edge your API request uses to ingress Twilio network, and the processing region for your request. Learn more about Edge Locations . Vanity URLs and security requirements vanity-urls-and-security-requirements page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Twilio has specific security requirements for accessing voice recording media files. Twilio doesn't support unauthenticated access to HTTP Voice recording media URLs using Canonical Name (CNAME) records. Use HTTPS endpoints and Transport-Layer-Security (TLS) protocols when accessing voice recordings media files from your account. For more information, see the Changelog (link takes you to an external page) . How the Twilio APIs handle webhooks how-the-twilio-apis-handle-webhooks page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Webhooks are user-defined HTTP callbacks triggered by an event in a web application. Twilio uses webhooks to let your application know when events happen, like getting an incoming call or receiving an SMS message. Webhooks are triggered asynchronously. When a webhook event occurs, Twilio makes an HTTP request, such as POST or GET , to the URL you configured for your webhook. Twilio's request to your application includes details of the event like the body of an incoming message or an incoming phone number. Your application can then process the event and reply to Twilio with a response containing the instructions you'd like Twilio to perform. To handle a webhook when you use Twilio, you need to build a web application that can accept HTTP requests. Check out the Twilio SDKs to get up and running quickly. Instead of a dollar-based balance, your trial includes transparent, product-specific free units — such as 100 SMS messages, 3,000 emails, and 75 voice minutes — so you know exactly what you can use. Each trial gives you a hands-on experience with real API requests and responses, so you can start building proofs of concept right away. Sign up for your Twilio trial account sign-up-for-your-twilio-trial-account page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Sign up for your Twilio account (link takes you to an external page) . The sign-up process includes the following steps: Verify your email address. Verify your personal phone number. Customize your account by providing information about your project. To get started, log in to the Twilio Console (link takes you to an external page) and select a product to try. Each trial walks you through setup, lets you send your first message or make your first call, and shows you the underlying API requests so you understand how Twilio works. When you're ready to go further, you can upgrade your account at any time to unlock full functionality. (information) Info You can sign up for a Twilio free trial account without a credit card. Trial accounts expire after 30 days. Upgrade your account before your trial expires to keep building. What you get with your Twilio trial what-you-get-with-your-twilio-trial page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Your trial includes free units for each product, rather than a shared dollar balance. The following table shows the free units included with your trial: Product Feature Free units Messaging SMS messages 100 Messaging WhatsApp messages 100 Voice Calls (minutes) 75 Voice Text-to-Speech Included Voice Speech Recognition Included Voice Answering Machine Detection Included Voice On-demand Conferencing Included Voice Transcriptions Included Email Emails 3,000 Verify Verifications 40 Lookup Lookups 100 During your trial, the features marked Included don't have separate unit tracking — they're covered by your Voice call minutes. Products that deliver over another channel deduct units from both counters. For example, sending a verification over SMS deducts one unit from your SMS messages. One unit is deducted from your verifications only after you successfully check the verification code. In the Console, click Free units tracker to see a summary of your current consumption and the percentage of units remaining. Available trials available-trials page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Try out SMS Messaging — Send and receive your first Twilio SMS messages within a few minutes. Try out Voice — Make and receive your first Twilio Voice calls within a few minutes. Try out Email — Send and receive your first Twilio Emails within a few minutes. Try out WhatsApp — Send and receive your first Twilio WhatsApp messages within a few minutes. Try out Verify — Send and check your first one-time passcode (OTP) verification within a few minutes. Try out Lookup — Perform your first phone number intelligence request within a few minutes. (information) Info RCS messaging is available after you upgrade your account. Trial restrictions trial-restrictions page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback 30-day expiration 30-day-expiration page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Trial accounts expire 30 days after sign-up. When your trial expires, you can no longer use trial resources. Upgrade your account to continue building. Geographic restrictions geographic-restrictions page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Trials are available in selected countries . SMS messages and voice calls are restricted to your sign-up country, determined by the phone number you used during registration. Email is restricted to the email address you used during sign-up. Verified recipients verified-recipients page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback You can send messages and make calls only to verified phone numbers. To verify a number, Twilio sends a verification code to that number. Each account can verify up to 5 recipients . Verified recipients are shared across Messaging, WhatsApp, Voice, and Verify, but trial numbers can vary by product and by recipient. The phone number you signed up with is automatically verified. A single verified recipient number can be associated with a maximum of three accounts globally. Pre-defined content pre-defined-content page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback You must use Twilio-provided templates or message examples. Custom message bodies, email content, and WhatsApp templates aren't available during the trial. SMS : Choose from pre-defined message templates such as order confirmations and appointment reminders. Custom message bodies are not supported. WhatsApp : Choose from pre-defined WhatsApp template messages. Custom WhatsApp templates are not supported. Email : Choose from pre-defined email templates. Custom email content is not supported. Voice : You can use Twilio-provided templates or custom TwiML with restrictions. Some TwiML verbs are blocked during trial. See Custom TwiML during trial for the full reference. Verify : Verifications use a Verify test template. Custom message bodies and custom code templates are not supported. Account limits and fraud prevention account-limits-and-fraud-prevention page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Trial free units are tracked at the parent account level. Subaccounts can use trial units, but they are granted and deducted at the parent account level. An organization is restricted to a maximum of 2 parent accounts with trial entitlements. Twilio trial numbers twilio-trial-numbers page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback Outgoing messages, calls, and conversations use a Twilio trial phone number. Trial numbers may differ between products and verified recipients in an account. Trial numbers are shared Twilio-owned numbers, not dedicated numbers assigned to your account. You can't keep your trial number when you upgrade. After you upgrade, purchase your own Twilio phone number to send messages and make calls. If you purchase a US Local or US/Canada Toll-free number, the first month is free. See Post-upgrade free unit allocations . For product-specific limitations, see the individual trial pages in the Available trials section. Upgrade your account upgrade-your-account page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback When you're ready to scale, upgrading is designed to be rewarding and low-friction. From the Console, click the Trial banner in the top left, or the Upgrade your account button on the right of the screen. Click Upgrade to perform your account upgrade. Alternatively, you can search for Upgrade in the Console search bar to find the upgrade page. Post-upgrade free units post-upgrade-free-units page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback When you upgrade, you automatically receive a fresh set of post-upgrade free units for eligible products, regardless of what you used during your trial. You're not required to opt-in. Twilio applies your free trial units to your usage before any charges begin. If a single usage event needs more units than you have left, Twilio bills that event at standard rates, and your remaining free units stay in your account for future usage. (information) Info After you upgrade, Twilio refreshes free units for eligible products. These post-upgrade free units help you continue building your proof of concept into a production application, or try another Twilio product without additional upfront cost. For example, if you used 20 of your 100 trial SMS messages before upgrading, you still receive another full set of free units after upgrade. Details: Automatic : Post-upgrade free units are granted immediately upon upgrade with no opt-in required. Parent account level : All free units (including post-upgrade free units) are awarded to parent accounts. Subaccounts can use these units, but they are granted and deducted at the parent account level. Sign-up upgrade bonus : If you upgrade your account directly during sign-up, you receive an additional 30% bonus on your post-upgrade free units. The bonus applies to all products except Twilio Conversations products and the free first month of a phone number. Twilio Conversations products : Post-upgrade free units for Conversations products, including Conversation Memory, Conversation Orchestrator, Enterprise Knowledge, and Conversation Intelligence, expire six months after first use. Twilio bills any usage after that period according to Twilio Conversations pricing (link takes you to an external page) . Your trial includes 30 active user months, so 15 users active for two months or 30 users active for one month would both use the full amount. Additional upgrade benefits additional-upgrade-benefits page anchor Positive Feedback Negative Feedback You're charged monthly according to current Voice (link takes you to an external page) and SMS (link takes you to an external page) rates after your free units are consumed. Verified recipient restrictions are removed. Custom message templates and TwiML become available. Multiple phone numbers become available. Conversations and other post-upgrade products become accessible.
